documents.text:
# Describing data
This lecture covers mean, median, mode, range, variance, standard deviation, outliers, quartiles, and the difference between a sample and a population.

## Mean
The arithmetic mean is the sum of the observations divided by their count. For 2, 3, 10 the mean is 5. Every value affects the mean, so an extreme observation can pull it toward that observation.

## Median
The median is the middle value after sorting the observations. For an odd count, use the single middle value. For an even count, average the two middle values. For 2, 3, 10 the median is 3. The median is less sensitive to the size of an extreme observation than the mean.

## Mode
The mode is a value with the highest frequency. A data set can have more than one mode. For 1, 1, 4, 4, 8 the modes are 1 and 4.

## Range
The range is the maximum minus the minimum. It uses only two observations and is sensitive to extremes. For 2, 3, 10 the range is 8.

## Variance and standard deviation
Variance describes average squared deviation from the mean. Population variance divides the sum of squared deviations by N. Sample variance divides it by n minus 1. Standard deviation is the square root of variance and has the same units as the original measurements; variance has squared units. For the population 2, 4, 6, the mean is 4, population variance is 8/3, and standard deviation is the square root of 8/3.

## Quartiles and interquartile range
Quartiles divide sorted data into four parts. Q2 is the median. The interquartile range is Q3 minus Q1 and describes the spread of the middle half of the observations. Different quartile conventions can give different results on small data sets, so state the convention when calculating them.

## Outliers
An outlier is an observation unusually far from the others. It may be an error or a real observation. Investigate its origin before deciding whether to remove it. Do not delete a value just because it is inconvenient.

## Sample and population
A population is the full group of interest. A sample is a subset observed to learn about that population. A sample statistic estimates a population parameter. Sampling bias can make a large sample unrepresentative.

Report A1 must contain 1800 words, excluding references. Submit it as a PDF by 18 November 2026 at 17:00 Asia/Seoul. Report A1 is worth 35 percent of the course grade. Do not confuse Report A1 with the optional Practice P1.

## Practice P1
Practice P1 is optional and ungraded. Its suggested length is 600 words. Upload a Markdown file by 11 November 2026 if you want feedback.

## Extension requests
A student may request an extension by emailing the teaching office at least 48 hours before the deadline. A request does not grant an extension; written approval is required. The handbook does not specify the maximum extension length.

## Study sessions
The suggested independent study session lasts 25 minutes followed by a 5 minute break. This is not an examination duration.

# Data structures and algorithms

## Stack
A stack removes the most recently added item first: last in, first out (LIFO). Push adds an item and pop removes the top item.

## Queue
A queue removes the earliest added item first: first in, first out (FIFO). Enqueue adds at the rear and dequeue removes from the front.

## Binary search
Binary search assumes the data are sorted and repeatedly halves the remaining search interval. It needs O(log n) comparisons. Applying the usual binary search algorithm to an unsorted list does not guarantee a correct result.

## Recursion
A recursive function calls itself. A base case stops the recursion, and recursive steps must move toward it. A missing base case or failure to make progress can lead to unbounded recursive calls.

## Example code
```python
def total(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return n + total(n - 1)
```
For a nonnegative integer n this function returns the sum from 1 through n. Negative inputs never reach the n == 0 base case.

## Precision and recall
For a classifier, precision is true positives divided by all predicted positives. Recall is true positives divided by all actual positives. False positives lower precision; false negatives lower recall.
